difficultyReason: The argument rests on a hidden methodological assumption: that absence of detected biomarkers in a controlled sample reliably reflects population-wide absence. The correct weakener attacks this unstated assumption rather than the surface causal claim. Distractors include a strengthener, a premise-level attack that doesn't touch the conclusion, and two out-of-scope comparisons.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical research team administered an experimental anti-inflammatory compound to 200 patients with chronic joint pain. After six months, blood tests detected no elevated inflammatory biomarkers in 87 percent of participants. The researchers concluded that the compound effectively suppresses chronic inflammation in the general patient population.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients with chronic joint pain who participated in the trial reported, on average, greater baseline pain levels than patients with the condition who did not participate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blood tests used to detect inflammatory biomarkers in the trial are calibrated to identify only the specific subset of biomarkers associated with one variety of chronic inflammation, leaving other varieties undetected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several competing anti-inflammatory compounds have failed to reduce biomarker levels in more than 70 percent of trial participants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some participants in the trial also modified their diets during the six-month period, which is known to independently reduce certain inflammatory biomarkers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The compound was found to be well-tolerated, with fewer than five percent of participants reporting adverse side effects.

explanations.correct: If some participants independently modified their diets—a change known to reduce inflammatory biomarkers—then the reduction in biomarkers may be attributable to dietary change rather than the compound. This introduces an alternative explanation that undermines the conclusion that the compound itself suppresses chronic inflammation.
explanations.A: This describes a self-selection effect regarding baseline pain but does not explain why the biomarker reductions might not be caused by the compound. It is largely irrelevant to the causal conclusion.
explanations.B: This is a tempting trap: it attacks the reliability of the measurement tool, but it actually implies the results might underestimate the compound's effectiveness (or simply that some inflammation went undetected). It does not show the compound fails to suppress inflammation—it is too narrow and arguably a premise-level attack that leaves the conclusion intact.
explanations.C: This is a strengthener trap: it implies the compound outperforms rivals, bolstering rather than weakening the conclusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable (dietary modification) that provides an alternative explanation for reduced biomarker levels.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Tolerability and side-effect profile bear on safety, not on whether the compound actually suppresses inflammation.

difficultyReason: The argument involves a two-step predictive chain: tax-credit expansion → increased private investment → reduced carbon emissions. The correct weakener attacks the second link in a way that requires recognizing the chain structure. Distractors include a choice that weakens only the first link and a strengthener that looks like an environmental concession.
stimulus: An economic policy analyst argued that expanding the federal tax credit for renewable energy installations would significantly reduce national carbon emissions over the next decade. Her reasoning was that the expanded credit would attract substantial private investment in wind and solar infrastructure, and that such infrastructure, once built, would displace a meaningful share of fossil-fuel-generated electricity on the national grid.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wind and solar installations funded through similar tax credits in two neighboring countries have consistently displaced fossil-fuel generation on those countries' grids.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several major private investors have publicly stated that they would increase renewable energy spending if the tax credit were expanded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grid operators have announced plans to retire a significant portion of coal-fired generating capacity within five years regardless of any new renewable installations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the national grid's transmission infrastructure cannot currently accommodate a rapid influx of distributed renewable generation, newly built wind and solar installations would largely sit idle rather than displace fossil-fuel output.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The existing federal tax credit for renewable energy has been criticized by some economists as an inefficient use of public funds.

explanations.correct: The analyst's conclusion depends on a chain: investment → built infrastructure → displaced fossil-fuel electricity. Choice D severs the second link: even if infrastructure is built, transmission constraints mean it cannot actually displace fossil-fuel output. This directly undermines the conclusion about emissions reduction.
explanations.A: This is a strengthener: analogous cases in neighboring countries support both causal links in the chain.
explanations.B: This is also a strengthener, confirming the first link (credit → investment) holds.
explanations.C: This is a 'too narrow / irrelevant' trap: it suggests emissions might fall anyway (which doesn't weaken the argument that the credit would reduce emissions—it merely introduces redundancy), but it does not attack the analyst's causal claim.
explanations.D: Correct. Severs the infrastructure-to-grid-displacement link, collapsing the conclusion.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: criticism of the existing (unexpanded) credit's efficiency does not bear on whether the expanded credit would achieve its emissions goal.

difficultyReason: The argument is an analogical one—drawing a conclusion about legal liability in one context based on precedent from a different context. The correct weakener identifies a structural disanalogy that undermines the analogy. Distractors include a choice that attacks a peripheral legal fact and a choice that strengthens the analogy.
stimulus: A legal scholar argued that municipalities should be held liable for injuries caused by potholes on public roads, citing the established precedent in which property owners are held liable for injuries caused by hazardous conditions on privately owned walkways. Since courts have consistently ruled that property owners who knew or should have known of a hazardous condition are responsible for resulting injuries, the same standard of constructive knowledge should impose liability on municipalities.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the legal scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Municipalities typically maintain far more linear miles of road surface than any private property owner maintains of walkway, making it practically impossible to inspect and remediate every hazardous condition within a reasonable time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts in several jurisdictions have extended private-property liability principles to commercial landlords who allow hazardous conditions to persist in common areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The constructive-knowledge standard for private-property liability has been applied consistently for more than forty years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some municipalities already carry insurance specifically designed to cover pothole-related injury claims.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Injuries resulting from pothole accidents are, on average, more severe than injuries resulting from walkway hazards on private property.

explanations.correct: The scholar's argument is analogical: because courts hold private property owners to a constructive-knowledge standard, municipalities should be held to the same standard. Choice A identifies a disanalogy—the sheer scale of public road networks makes it structurally impossible for municipalities to satisfy a constructive-knowledge standard in the same way a private owner can. This disanalogy weakens the basis for transferring the liability rule.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: it shows courts have already expanded the private-property liability principle beyond its original context, supporting the scholar's analogical extension.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: the longevity of the standard does not bear on whether it can be validly applied to municipalities.
explanations.D: Irrelevant: the existence of insurance does not affect whether the legal liability standard should apply; it neither strengthens nor weakens the analogy.
explanations.E: This is a 'shift in subject' trap: injury severity is irrelevant to whether the constructive-knowledge standard should apply; it does not address the validity of the analogy.

difficultyReason: The argument generalizes from a controlled linguistic experiment to a universal cognitive claim. The correct weakener identifies a methodological flaw in the sample's representativeness that the conclusion silently assumes away. Distractors include a choice that trivially weakens one datum point without affecting the generalization and a reversed-causation trap.
stimulus: Linguists at a research institute conducted a study in which monolingual English-speaking adults were asked to arrange photographs of events in chronological order without verbal instruction. Participants consistently arranged the photographs from left to right, suggesting that the directional bias instilled by reading left-to-right scripts causes people to conceptualize time as flowing from left to right.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A small number of the monolingual English-speaking participants in the study had previously been exposed to right-to-left scripts through casual contact with foreign-language media.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When the same photograph-arrangement task was administered to monolingual speakers of Arabic—a right-to-left script language—those participants consistently arranged the photographs from right to left.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the photographs used in the study depicted events that carry culturally specific temporal associations likely familiar only to participants raised in English-speaking environments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurological research has established that a left-to-right directional preference in spatial tasks originates in hemisphere dominance patterns present at birth, before any exposure to written scripts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some languages that use left-to-right scripts also employ vertical text layouts in certain formal contexts.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that reading left-to-right scripts causes the left-to-right temporal bias. Choice D offers neurological evidence that the directional preference exists at birth—before script exposure—which undermines the causal direction claimed and suggests the correlation is not driven by reading habits at all.
explanations.A: This is a 'too narrow' trap: a small number of participants with peripheral exposure barely dents the study's findings and does not challenge the causal conclusion for the broader population.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: it shows that speakers of a right-to-left language arrange time in the opposite direction, directly supporting the claim that script directionality causes temporal conceptualization.
explanations.C: This attacks the experimental design at a narrow level (photo familiarity), but even if some photos were culturally loaded, this doesn't undermine the causal claim about script directionality—it's a premise-level distractor that leaves the conclusion largely intact.
explanations.D: Correct. Provides an alternative, pre-linguistic causal origin for the observed bias, directly undermining the conclusion that script exposure is the cause.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: the existence of vertical layouts in some left-to-right languages is irrelevant to whether reading directionality causes temporal conceptualization patterns.

difficultyReason: The conclusion overreaches from a historical correlation to a causal policy prescription. The hidden assumption—that the historical mechanism still operates under current conditions—is attacked by the correct answer. Multiple distractors are carefully calibrated: one weakens a peripheral fact, one strengthens, and one is an accurate but temporally mislocated fact.
stimulus: A historian argued that government investment in public university systems historically preceded periods of sustained economic growth in industrialized nations. Citing data from fifteen countries over the twentieth century, she concluded that expanding public university enrollment today would generate comparable economic growth in the coming decades.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In several of the fifteen countries studied, the periods of economic growth the historian identified were also accompanied by significant expansions of transportation infrastructure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The economic growth that followed public university expansion in the twentieth century was driven primarily by demand for graduates trained in manufacturing-sector skills that are now almost entirely automated, making such graduates no longer a significant driver of economic output.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public universities in industrialized nations today enroll a substantially higher proportion of the college-age population than they did at the start of the twentieth century.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some private universities in industrialized nations have recently increased tuition at rates that exceed inflation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fifteen countries the historian studied represent a geographically and economically diverse sample of industrialized nations.

explanations.correct: The historian's argument assumes the same mechanism that connected university expansion to economic growth historically will still operate today. Choice B shows that the mechanism—graduate labor in manufacturing—is now largely automated and no longer drives economic output. This severs the causal link between university expansion and economic growth under current conditions, directly weakening the conclusion.
explanations.A: This introduces a confounding variable for the historical correlation (transportation infrastructure), which is a valid weakener of the historical data—but only trivially, because it attacks the historical premise rather than the move from historical evidence to the current policy conclusion. The conclusion's main vulnerability is the applicability of the historical mechanism today.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the hidden assumption that the historical mechanism still applies.
explanations.C: This is a 'too narrow' trap: higher current enrollment might suggest diminishing returns, but it doesn't directly explain why the mechanism would fail; it merely notes a baseline difference. It does not strongly undermine the conclusion.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: private university tuition is irrelevant to the effects of expanding public university enrollment.
explanations.E: This is a strengthener: sample diversity supports the generalizability of the historian's data.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves an ethical argument whose conclusion depends on an unstated principle about moral responsibility. The correct weakener attacks this hidden normative premise. Distractors include a choice that concedes the factual premise while leaving the normative conclusion untouched, and a strengthener framed in sympathetic moral language.
stimulus: A bioethicist argued that pharmaceutical companies that hold patents on life-saving medications bear a moral obligation to supply those medications at cost to low-income patients in developing nations. Her reasoning was that the companies' research was substantially funded by government grants—that is, by the public—and that entities benefiting from public resources are morally obligated to make the products of that benefit available to the public at cost.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the bioethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several pharmaceutical companies already operate voluntary access programs that supply certain life-saving medications below cost in developing nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The government grants that funded the relevant research were awarded competitively and did not guarantee that the resulting discoveries would be patentable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The costs of clinical trials, regulatory approval, and manufacturing scale-up—none of which are covered by the research grants—constitute the majority of the total investment required to bring a pharmaceutical to market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Access to life-saving medications is recognized as a fundamental human right in numerous international legal instruments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some pharmaceutical patents cover medications that are not life-saving but are instead used to treat conditions that are merely uncomfortable.

explanations.correct: The bioethicist's normative principle is: entities that benefit from public resources are obligated to provide the resulting products at cost to the public. Choice C shows that the companies' obligations arise largely from private investment (clinical trials, regulatory costs, manufacturing), not from the public grants. This undermines the factual basis for the normative principle—the companies' product is not primarily the product of public benefit—and so weakens the conclusion that they owe an at-cost obligation.
explanations.A: This is irrelevant to the argument's logical validity: voluntary programs don't address whether the obligation exists; they describe a behavior some companies already exhibit, leaving the conclusion unaffected.
explanations.B: This attacks a peripheral element (the foreseeability of the patent) without bearing on whether the companies actually benefited from public resources—the core premise. It's too narrow.
explanations.C: Correct. Undermines the premise that the companies' product is primarily the result of public benefit, thereby attacking the normative principle's factual foundation.
explanations.D: This is a strengthener framed in sympathetic moral language: recognizing medication access as a human right lends additional support to the bioethicist's conclusion.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope and involves a 'shift in subject' trap: the argument is about life-saving medications specifically; the existence of non-life-saving patents is irrelevant.

difficultyReason: The argument is a predictive one based on ecological modeling. The conclusion depends on an assumption about the reliability of the model's parameters under changed conditions. The correct weakener attacks this hidden methodological assumption. The distractors include a strengthener that cites analogous past success, a narrowly scoped choice, and an out-of-scope comparison.
stimulus: Environmental scientists at a federal agency used a computational model to predict that reintroducing gray wolves to a national forest would, within twenty years, reduce the overpopulation of white-tailed deer by 40 percent, thereby allowing native vegetation to recover to pre-settlement density levels. The model's projections are based on wolf predation rates and deer population dynamics observed in a separate national park where wolves were reintroduced a decade ago.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national forest targeted for wolf reintroduction is bordered on three sides by privately owned agricultural land where wolves would be subject to legal lethal control, a condition not present in the national park used to calibrate the model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: White-tailed deer in the national forest have shown signs of nutritional stress, suggesting that the current population may be near the upper limit of what the forest's food resources can sustain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wolf reintroduction programs in two other national parks have produced deer population reductions broadly consistent with the model's predictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The native vegetation in the national forest includes several plant species that are not present in the national park where wolf predation data were collected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gray wolves typically require territories larger than the boundaries of the national forest, meaning individual packs may range into adjacent areas.

explanations.correct: The model's validity depends on applying parameters from one setting (the reference national park) to the target forest. Choice A identifies a structural difference—wolf mortality from lethal control on adjacent private land—that would reduce the wolf population well below the levels the model assumes, undermining the projection that wolves will reduce deer by 40 percent.
explanations.B: This is a 'too narrow / opposite direction' trap: nutritional stress in deer might independently reduce the deer population, which if anything would make the 40% reduction goal easier to achieve—a slight strengthener.
explanations.C: This is a strengthener: corroborating evidence from two other parks supports the model's reliability.
explanations.D: This is a plausible-sounding distractor, but different plant species affect vegetation recovery patterns rather than wolf predation rates or deer population dynamics—the parameters the model actually uses. It is out-of-scope relative to the conclusion about deer reduction.
explanations.E: This is an 'accurate but irrelevant' trap: wolves ranging outside the forest boundary could reduce effective predation within the forest (a mild weakener), but the more significant structural difference is the lethal-control issue in choice A. More importantly, ranging behavior was presumably observable at the reference park as well.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a technology policy argument. The conclusion relies on an unstated assumption about the representativeness of a pilot program. The correct weakener attacks this assumption by revealing a selection effect. Distractors include a premise-level attack that doesn't reach the conclusion and a reversed-scope trap.
stimulus: A government technology advisory board recommended that all public secondary schools nationwide adopt tablet-based learning platforms, citing a pilot program in which students at twelve schools that voluntarily adopted the platforms showed a 22 percent improvement in standardized test scores over two years. The board concluded that nationwide adoption would produce comparable improvements across the secondary school population.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the advisory board's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The twelve schools that volunteered for the pilot program were selected from among those that had already applied for technology-upgrade grants, indicating they had unusually motivated administrative staff and strong existing technology infrastructure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standardized tests used to measure student performance in the pilot program were developed by the same company that manufactures the tablet-based learning platforms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several industrialized nations that have implemented nationwide tablet-based learning have reported mixed results, with some showing score improvements and others showing no significant change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost of equipping all public secondary schools with the tablets and associated software would require a substantial reallocation of existing education budgets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teachers at the twelve pilot schools received extensive professional development training prior to the platform rollout.

explanations.correct: The board's conclusion assumes the pilot schools are representative of all secondary schools. Choice A reveals a selection effect—the pilot schools had unusually motivated staff and robust infrastructure, conditions unlikely to hold nationwide. This undermines the generalization from pilot results to population-wide outcomes.
explanations.B: This is tempting: it attacks the reliability of the test scores measured during the pilot. However, it is a 'premise attack' trap—it questions whether the 22% improvement was real, not whether that improvement would generalize. Even if we accept the 22% improvement as real, the selection-effect problem in choice A more directly attacks the conclusion about nationwide adoption.
explanations.C: This introduces mixed international evidence, which is a weak weakener at best—'mixed results' abroad doesn't clearly undermine adoption in a specific national context. It's also out-of-scope relative to the specific pilot data cited.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: cost and budget reallocation bear on the practicality of the recommendation, not on whether the conclusion (comparable improvements) would hold if adopted.
explanations.E: This is a 'too narrow' trap: it identifies another confounding factor (professional development) that may have contributed to the improvement, but it does not directly attack the representativeness of the pilot schools or the generalizability of the conclusion.

difficultyReason: The argument uses an artifact analysis to draw a historical conclusion about cultural diffusion. The conclusion's hidden assumption—that the artifact type is unique to one culture—is what the correct answer attacks. Distractors include a strengthener disguised as an archaeological nuance and an irrelevant temporal fact.
stimulus: An archaeologist argued that a Bronze Age culture from the eastern Mediterranean was responsible for introducing a distinctive style of bronze fibula—a type of decorative clasp—to communities in central Europe. Her evidence was that fibulae of this precise style have been excavated at sites in central Europe that also contain pottery shards dated to the period of known maritime trade between the two regions. She concluded that the central European fibulae were trade goods originating in the eastern Mediterranean culture.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the archaeologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronze fibulae of the same distinctive style have been independently produced by metalworking communities in central Europe since at least a century before the period of documented eastern Mediterranean maritime trade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pottery shards found alongside the fibulae at the central European sites are of a type that eastern Mediterranean traders are known to have exported widely during the relevant period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the central European sites where the fibulae were excavated show evidence of having been occupied continuously for more than five hundred years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bronze fibulae of other styles found at the same central European sites have been attributed to local production rather than trade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The eastern Mediterranean culture that the archaeologist identifies as the origin of the fibulae was itself a significant importer of raw bronze from central European sources.

explanations.correct: The archaeologist's conclusion depends on the assumption that the distinctive fibula style originated in the eastern Mediterranean and was brought to central Europe via trade. Choice A undermines this by showing that central European metalworkers produced the same style independently before the trade contact even began—eliminating the eastern Mediterranean origin as a necessary explanation.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: it confirms that the associated pottery is consistent with eastern Mediterranean trade exports, corroborating the trade-goods hypothesis.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: continuous occupation of a site is irrelevant to whether a particular artifact style arrived via trade or was locally produced.
explanations.D: This is a 'too narrow' trap: it shows that some fibulae at the sites are locally made, but it doesn't address the specific style at issue. It slightly undermines the argument by suggesting local production is possible, but it fails to show the distinctive style was locally produced.
explanations.E: This introduces a reversed-trade direction (central Europe exported bronze to the east), which is interesting but irrelevant to whether the distinctive fibula style traveled east-to-west via trade. It's an 'accurate but irrelevant' distractor.

difficultyReason: The argument is a policy argument about arts funding whose conclusion depends on a hidden assumption about the stability of the relationship between funding and attendance. The correct weakener attacks this by showing that the mechanism that produced the observed correlation has reversed. Multiple distractors exploit the student's tendency to accept surface-level plausibility.
stimulus: A city arts council presented data showing that over the past fifteen years, public funding for municipal theater programs correlated strongly with increases in theater attendance. The council concluded that increasing public arts funding by 30 percent in the next budget cycle would produce a significant rise in theater attendance citywide.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the arts council's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Survey data indicate that the primary reason theater attendance increased over the past fifteen years was not the funded productions themselves but rather the renovation of several theater buildings, a project now fully completed with no further renovations planned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theater attendance in cities that did not increase public arts funding remained flat over the same fifteen-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 30 percent funding increase would be financed through a reallocation of funds currently used to support municipal music programs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of the municipal theaters that received public funding over the past fifteen years have recently experienced increases in private sponsorship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economists who specialize in cultural policy have argued that arts funding produces social benefits beyond attendance figures, such as civic identity and neighborhood revitalization.

explanations.correct: The council's argument assumes that the mechanism driving the past correlation—funding → attendance—will continue to operate. Choice A reveals that the actual driver of attendance growth was building renovation, not funded productions. Since those renovations are complete with none planned, the mechanism is exhausted; additional funding will not replicate the past attendance gains.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: flat attendance in cities without funding increases supports the council's implied claim that funding (not other factors) caused attendance to rise.
explanations.C: This is an 'adjacent-harm' trap: it raises a concern about the funding reallocation's effect on music programs, but this does not bear on whether the theater funding increase would raise theater attendance—the council's actual conclusion.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: increases in private sponsorship are consistent with either the argument or its negation; they don't address whether additional public funding will raise attendance.
explanations.E: This is a 'shift in subject' trap: social benefits beyond attendance are irrelevant to the council's specific conclusion about attendance figures. If anything, it subtly supports the council's general pro-funding position, making it a mild strengthener on an adjacent claim.
